Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:40: Further, he comes to resolve a difficulty: one might ask, what does he come to teach us by [saying] that silence is good, since in several verses of King Solomon, peace be upon him, the matter of silence is already mentioned — "he who restrains his words has knowledge" (Proverbs 17:27), "therefore let your words be few" (Ecclesiastes 5:1), and many similar verses? To this he says, "not the study is the essential thing" — meaning, my intent in saying "I have found nothing better for the body than silence" is that I read Solomon's words and fulfilled them, and so it is fitting for whoever reads King Solomon's words to fulfill them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:41: The same applies to all matters where "not the study is the essential thing," and so on — rather, this quality is a key to them. The reason is that whoever becomes accustomed to silence, not uttering a word in vain out of fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, who are the inner essence of the neshamah, being voice and speech, will benefit thereby in the intention of his prayer, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains in the Tikkunim (3a), that one must intend, in every place and every utterance, voice and speech, the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:42: Since he has become accustomed, in worldly matters, not to utter voice and speech in vain, all the more so will he not utter them in vain during his prayer. Therefore they instituted, at the end [of the Amidah], "My God, guard my tongue from evil" — the intent following what was explained above, that one who utters a word in vain is like one who emits seed in vain, called "evil"; and if a person guards himself in worldly matters from uttering a word in vain, all the more so in his prayer. And if, God forbid, he is blemished in his tongue, his prayer does not ascend above, for it is subdued beneath that [Other] side, as is explained in Parashat Pekudei (263b), whose wording we shall quote below in chapter 13 regarding blemish.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:43: Likewise it brings one to humility and awe together, when he considers what we explained regarding the verse, "and let not your heart be hasty to utter a word before God" (Ecclesiastes 5:1) — that when he considers that he stands before the Name, blessed be He, he should not respond to his own disgrace, as King David, peace be upon him, said, "for in You, O Lord, do I hope" (Psalms 38:16), and this is "my soul is silent," and so on; and his voice will be low, for he will be ashamed to raise his voice before the King. And in considering always that his neshamah is attached to its root, he will strive to occupy himself with Torah and commandments for the honor of his father and mother, and to do their will, as explained in the Tikkunim (146b) regarding "honor your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12), which we quoted in the Gate of Love. He will also strive not to cause any blemish, since by blemishing he blemishes the supernal roots. This matter will cause him to repent of all his sins, in order to purify his neshamah so that it may cling to its root; and it will cause him to purify his thoughts, since he will be ashamed to think anything against His service, blessed be He, because the Name, blessed be He, is watching and is within him, in the manner explained. And since he is attached to the Tree of Life, he will be strong in trust, that nothing of worldly matters will harm him, and that he is always watched over from above, as it is said, "Behold, the eye of the Lord is upon those who fear Him..." (Psalms 33:18). It follows that the acquisition of this quality is the root for the fulfillment of the entire Torah, because once he knows it in its mystery, as explained, he will fulfill it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:44: Further, regarding the greatness of silence, the Tanna says (Avot 3:13), "a fence for wisdom is silence." The meaning is: just as tithes are a fence for wealth — since to attain wealth one must tithe, as is explained (Shabbat 119a), "aser te'aser" ("you shall surely tithe") (Deuteronomy 14:22) — tithe so that you may become wealthy — and so with the other fences mentioned in the Mishnah, they follow this pattern — so too, for a person to attain wisdom, it is impossible except through acquiring the quality of silence. And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explain (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:21), that from a Torah scholar who speaks idle words, words of Torah leave him — we shall quote their wording in the next chapter. In this manner one might say the reason is that through his silence he removes himself from the activity of the six extremities, which are voice and speech, and ascends to the place of silence, which is Thought, the mystery of Chochmah, as it says (Menachot 29b), "be silent, thus it arose in thought."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:45: Further, the reason is that since a person is silent, he makes himself a chariot for the place of silence, and merits having bestowed upon him the secrets of Torah that are in silence, not given over to be revealed, as they say in the Zohar several times (Parashat Emor 105b). And one of the forty-eight things through which Torah is acquired is minimizing conversation, and so on (Avot 6:6).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:46: Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in the Midrash Yelamdenu, said regarding "and Miriam and Aaron spoke..." (Numbers 12:1): this is what the verse says, "in the multitude of words there is no lack of transgression, but he who restrains his lips is wise" (Proverbs 10:19) — whoever restrains his lips from speaking about his fellow is wise. Rabban Gamliel said, all my days I grew up among the Sages, and I have found nothing better for the body than silence. Our Rabbis said: two rhetoricians stood before Hadrian; one of them taught in favor of speech, that it is good, and one taught in favor of silence. The one said to him, "My lord, there is nothing better than speech — without speech, how would brides be praised, how would there be commerce in the world, how would ships spread out on the sea?" Immediately he said to the one who taught in favor of silence being good [to speak]. He immediately came to speak; the one who taught in favor of speech got up and slapped him. The king said to him, "Why did you slap him?" He said to him, "What I taught was in favor of speech regarding speech, and this one came to teach my example in favor of his own [silence, by speaking]!" Solomon said: the Holy One, blessed be He, did not say that you should conceal your mouth and sit silent as a deaf-mute, but rather, "he restrains his lips" from talking about his fellow — pay attention that you not be punished. There is none greater than Aaron and Miriam — the well rose and gave drink to Israel by Miriam's merit, and clouds of glory surrounded Israel by Aaron's merit — yet since they permitted their mouths and spoke against Moses, I did not remain silent toward them — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:47: At first glance this passage seems to contradict the words of Rabbi Yitzchak that we quoted in the preceding chapter, who said (Chullin 89a), "what is a person's occupation in this world? He should make himself as one silent," as it is said, "do you indeed speak righteousness, you silent ones" (Psalms 58:2). And this passage says that the matter of silence is [only] restraining one's lips from talking about one's fellow — implying that regarding everything else, a person is permitted to speak at length about his own affairs, business, and dealings, and the like.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:48: One might say that when we are precise about its words, saying, "the Holy One, blessed be He, did not say that you should conceal your mouth and sit silent as a deaf-mute, but rather, he restrains his lips," and so on, we find it to be a passage in harmony with, and not contradicting at all, the words of Rabbi Yitzchak.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:49: The matter is that the Midrash Yelamdenu comes to explain the verse, "in the multitude of words there is no lack of transgression, but he who restrains his lips is wise" — for it is impossible to explain Solomon's words as going from one extreme to the other: "in the multitude of words there is no lack of transgression" [implying total silence is the ideal], and "restrains his lips" referring to complete silence, which would be the ultimate extreme — rather, "restrains his lips" is the intermediate quality, that he restrains his lips from speaking about his fellow. And the word "restrains" (chosech) suggests that even though there is some benefit in speaking, nevertheless it is better not to speak — for behold, Miriam intended for the sake of Heaven, to be fruitful and multiply, as we shall quote from the passage of the Sifrei below, and even so she was punished — this being [the sense of] "restrain" in a place where there is [some justification] to speak. Nevertheless, reason dictates that if he is forced to speak regarding matters of buying and selling, he should speak; therefore it says, "the Holy One, blessed be He, did not say that you should conceal your mouth and sit silent as a deaf-mute" — that a person should say, since "in the multitude of words there is no lack of transgression," and the transgression is certainly speaking about one's fellow and the like, "I will sit as a deaf-mute so as not to come to this, and I will cease from dealing and trading with people" — to this Solomon comes and says "restrains his lips," meaning from talking about his fellow, to qualify what he said at the beginning of the verse, "in the multitude of words there is no lack of transgression" — such a person is called "wise" (maskil), for he has the sense to speak where it is fitting to speak, and his intellect overpowers his inclination and prevents him from speaking where it is not fitting. It is further possible that he is called "maskil" because speech is in the place of the female, and above her is "maskil le'Eitan ha'Ezrachi" (Psalms 89:1), and so on, as explained in Sabba (Parashat Mishpatim 110a-b); and the difference between male and female is that things depend on the male in the intellect, in concealment, and on the female in speech — that is, in revelation. And since he is called "maskil," fortunate is he, for he is among those of whom it is said, "and the wise (maskilim) shall shine like the brightness of the firmament" (Daniel 12:3), as is elaborated in the Tikkunim in manuscript — that no mystery is beyond them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:50: There is a third division: silence in matters where a person is not speaking about his fellow — such as lengthy talk in tales of kings and parables of common people, and the like, lengthening speech in what is not absolutely necessary for one's dealings; since there is no benefit in these, there is no need to say "restrain" as explained, but rather it is certainly forbidden, since it is said, "all things are wearisome, man cannot express it" (Ecclesiastes 1:8), as will be explained below. King Solomon, peace be upon him, mentioned this division explicitly in the verse, "he who restrains (chosech) his words has knowledge" (Proverbs 17:27); and the pious author explains that "restrains his words" refers to one who has a need to speak, and yet restrains himself, as we quoted his wording above; and he connects this to the following verse (Proverbs 17:28), "even a fool, when he holds his peace, is counted wise; he who shuts (otem) his lips is esteemed a man of understanding." Certainly the words "holds his peace" and "shuts" cannot be explained as referring to holding one's peace or shutting one's lips from speaking about one's fellow, for this was not mentioned in the verse; and if this were the intent, why would King Solomon, peace be upon him, need to repeat his words, since it was already said above, "restrains his lips is wise"? Rather, certainly he comes to teach us the matter that Rabbi Akiva says in the Mishnah, "a fence for wisdom is silence" — that even in what pertains to one's own needs, one must be silent; the explanation is that he should not prolong his speech, and a matter that seems to him to have some justification for speaking and some justification for not speaking, but is not so necessary, it is better not to speak — this is what it says in the Midrash, "a word is worth a sela, silence is worth two." The reason is that the quality of silence is in the quality of Chochmah, as explained — this being [the meaning of] "even a fool, when he holds his peace, is counted wise" — for he has grasped the quality of Chochmah, as we elaborated above on the mystery of speech. But whoever prolongs his words in worldly matters holds onto Malchut, which governs the world, where speech is — for "ten measures of conversation descended to the world, nine were taken by women" (Kiddushin 49b), and this is the aspect of the Shechinah nesting in the Ofan (see Tikkunei Zohar 23a) — that he not become wise.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:51: There is an aspect of blemished speech corresponding to Asiyah, where the kelipot are, such as evil speech, gossip, idle talk, and the like; and therefore it is said, "whoever breaks through a fence, a serpent shall bite him" (Ecclesiastes 10:8) — this refers to one who breaks through the fences of the tongue's walls, just as the serpent always stands between fences and broke through the fence of the world, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explain (Bamidbar Rabbah 19:2): Rabbi Shimon bar Nachmani said, they asked the serpent and said to him, "Why are you found among the fences?" He said to them, "Because I broke through the fence of the world." They said to him, "Why does your tongue trail on the ground?" He said to them, "It caused me to speak evil against my Creator." And what was the evil speech he spoke? Rabbi Yehoshua of Sichnin said in the name of Reish Lakish: the first serpent used to speak like human beings; once Adam and Eve did not wish to eat from that tree, he began to speak evil against his Creator, saying to them, "From this tree the Creator ate and created His world, and He commanded you not to eat from it so that you would not create worlds like His." What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He cut off its legs and cut off its tongue so that it could not speak. They asked the serpent, "What do you gain when you bite?" He said to them, "Rather than ask me, ask the master of evil speech" — as it is written, "if a serpent bites without being charmed, then there is no advantage for the charmer" (Ecclesiastes 10:11) — what does he gain when he speaks evil speech? They said to the serpent, "Why do you bite in one limb, yet your venom travels through all the limbs?" He said to them, "Rather than ask me, ask the master of evil speech, who speaks evil speech in Rome and kills in Syria" — so far their words. Thus the master of the tongue is likened to the serpent in every aspect; it follows that he descends to the place of the kelipot and breaks through the fences of holiness and lets the outsider in, as will be further explained regarding the sin of evil speech.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:52: What emerges from the whole of this chapter is that guarding the tongue from anything that blemishes it is necessary, whether evil speech, vulgarity, or idle talk. We have elaborated on the greatness of silence, because since a person is distinguished in his speech from the beasts and animals and is equal to the angels, it is fitting that he sanctify his speech, as it says in the Yerushalmi (Berachot 9:5), "all chatter is bad except the chatter of Torah, which is good." And it further says in the Yerushalmi (Berachot 1:2): Rabbi Levi said, if I had been at Mount Sinai I would have asked for two mouths — for in the mouth that is fitting to speak words of Torah and praise and thanksgiving, it is not fitting to speak words of this world, all the more so a blemishing matter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:53: A person's mouth was created only to occupy itself with Torah, as we learn in the chapter Chelek (Sanhedrin 99b): Rabbi Elazar says, man was created for toil, and I do not know whether it is for the toil of his mouth or another toil; when it says, "his mouth compels him" (Proverbs 16:26), you may say the mouth was created for toil; but I still do not know whether for the toil of Torah or the toil of conversation — when it says, "this book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth" (Joshua 1:8), you may say it was created for the toil of Torah — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:54: One of the authors who speak of matters of piety speaks well on the subject of silence, and I have seen fit to quote his words, in these words: and it happened that Rabban Gamliel made a feast, and told his servant to prepare several kinds of dishes, and gave him money to purchase the needs of the feast. The servant went and bought several tongues, and made some of them roasted and some cooked, some soft and some tough. He brought before them the cooked ones and then brought the roasted ones; he brought before them the soft ones and then brought before them the tough ones. Rabban Gamliel called the servant and said to him, "What made you do this — some are tough and some are soft, and also roasted and cooked?" He said to him, "To let you know that everything is in the hand of the tongue, for sometimes it is good and soft, and sometimes it is bad or tough; if a person wishes, he does good with it, and if he wishes, he does evil with it."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:55: There was also a story of a certain king who had several counselors — wise, discerning, and knowledgeable men. Once the king saw that one of them, who was the wisest of them, was sitting silent and quiet. The king said to him, "Why is it that you engage in so much silence?" He said to him, "Because I examined matters, and found that they divide into four categories: the first is entirely harm; the second is harm on one side and benefit on the other; the third is neither harm nor benefit; the fourth is entirely benefit. The first — such as people accustomed to cursing others. The second — praising a person to gain benefit from him, and in that same praise disparaging his enemy, harming the one who is praised [by association]. The third, neither harm nor benefit — such as those accustomed to speaking idle words and vain talk — how was so-and-so's house built, and how much did he spend on it, and tales of kings and princes, and such and such. The fourth — such as Torah and the Prophets, where lives depend on lives."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:56: There are Torah scholars who divide these four into five categories: one, a commandment to speak it; two, one must be careful of it; three, it is repugnant; four, it is beloved; five, it is permitted. One, a commandment — such as speaking words of Torah and fear of Heaven. Two, one must be careful of it — such as false testimony, gossip, and vulgar speech. Three, repugnant — that which has neither transgression nor benefit for the most part, such as speaking of things already done, the customs of kings, and various matters of this world. And although the wise man said there is neither transgression nor benefit in this, another sage said there is transgression in it and no benefit. Four, the beloved — this is one who speaks in praise of good deeds and condemns evil deeds, praising the righteous so that their good practices be viewed favorably by people and that others follow their ways, and condemning the wicked so that they be scorned and despised in people's eyes, so that their memory be erased and people distance themselves from them and not follow their practices. Five, the permitted — this is speech about commerce and livelihood, speaking of clothing matters and eating and drinking and other needs; and whoever minimizes his words even in this matter is praiseworthy. According to the words of the Sages, most worldly talk has no need to be spoken.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:57: There are things it is greatly forbidden to speak of, such as mockery, flattery, and speaking evil speech — and regarding these four, a separate gate should be written for each one.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:58: In several circumstances silence is good — such as if the attribute of Judgment befalls one, as Aaron did, as it is said, "and Aaron was silent" (Leviticus 10:3). And if a person hears his own disgrace and does not respond, this is a great commandment and a supernal virtue — to be silent toward those who disgrace him. Also, a person should accustom himself to being silent in the synagogue, and this is his modesty; and this requires great zeal — to be silent in the synagogue and refrain from speaking even words of Torah, and all the more so other matters — all so that he can direct his heart to prayer. And if he sits silent among his companions and listens to their words, it is good when he is silent and hears what he did not know; and when he speaks, he does not add knowledge. But if he is uncertain about the words of the Sages, he should ask them, for this kind of silence is very bad.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:59: King Solomon said, "a time to keep silent and a time to speak" (Ecclesiastes 3:7), for sometimes silence is good and sometimes speech is good. And the sage said: when you do not find a man who has taught you moral discipline, cling to silence, lest you speak folly. Since the tongue is quick to speak, one must very much slow down the tongue and guard it so as not to multiply words, for a multitude of words is like a burden, and the heaviness of a multitude of words is heavier than the heaviness of much silence. If he hears his fellow speaking, he should be silent until he finishes his words; and so Solomon said, "he who answers a matter before he hears it, it is folly and shame to him" (Proverbs 18:13).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:60: Whoever is accustomed to silence is saved from several transgressions — from insults and curses, from evil speech, from mockery, from lies — for when a person is insulted and cursed by his fellow, if he responds, he will provoke [his fellow] to speak to him even more. And so the sage said: I hear evil spoken of me and I am silent. They said to him, "Why?" He said to them, "If I respond to my insulters, I fear I will hear other insults harsher than the first." And he said, when a fool argues with a wise man and the wise man is silent, this is a great response to the fool, for the fool is more distressed by the wise man's silence than if he had responded to him; and concerning this it is said, "Do not answer a fool according to his folly" (Proverbs 26:4). Further, a person may reveal secrets to him since he is not accustomed to much talk and will not reveal a secret, for a person does more with his tongue than with his sword — for a person stands here and hands over his fellow, far away from him, to death, whereas with a sword he can only kill someone close to him. Therefore man was created with two ears, two eyes, and two nostrils, but one mouth — to indicate that he should minimize his speech.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:61: Silence is fitting for the wise, all the more so for fools (Pesachim 99a), and "a fence for wisdom is silence." But sometimes silence is bad, as it is written, "answer a fool according to his folly" (Proverbs 26:5) — regarding words of Torah, if you see that fools are casting their words upon matters of Torah, answer them to correct their error. If a person sees another committing a transgression, he should raise his hand and rebuke him; and Solomon already said, "a soft answer turns away wrath" (Proverbs 15:1); therefore every person should accustom himself to having soft words, and not be accustomed to harsh words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:62: Be careful with your tongue to guard it as the pupil of the eye, as it is said, "whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles" (Proverbs 21:23). If you sit in company, it is good that they say to you, "Speak!" — and even if they insult you, it is better that you be silent, rather than speaking and your words becoming a burden to them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:63: He should be very careful not to shame a person or cause distress with his words. If he sits near a person who has a physical blemish he is ashamed of, or a blemish in his children or wife, or a defect in his family, he should be very careful not to speak of that blemish or defect, even if he is not speaking about him but about another person who has this blemish — for he will always think it is spoken about him and will be ashamed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:64: If a person did something disgraceful and repented and returns [to good ways], he should also be careful not to speak of that matter before him, or say to him, even jokingly, "How could you have done that, and why weren't you careful of it?" — even this he should not do, for he thereby shames him. If a person tells you words of Torah that you already know, be silent until he finishes the matter, for perhaps he will introduce something new that you did not know from the start; and also he takes pleasure in telling you the matter — and even if you know that nothing new will be revealed to you, be silent for him until he speaks and finishes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:65: Two people who had a quarrel with each other, and afterward reconciled, neither of them should say, "You did such-and-such to me, and therefore I did such-and-such to you," even if he has no intention of returning to their dispute — for by saying, "You did such-and-such to me," his fellow will respond, "On the contrary, the whole fault was yours!" and thereby the quarrel will be aroused again; and even if the quarrel is not aroused, the one who was at fault will be shamed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:66: One who sits before a sage and is silent has a reward, such as when he intends to listen; and there is one who is silent and has a transgression — such as thinking, "What shall I say before him, since he does not know how to answer me properly, does he not know anything compared to me?" He should be very careful of what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 5:7): seven things characterize a clod, and seven characterize a wise man. A wise man does not speak before one greater than him in wisdom or in age; does not interrupt his fellow's words; is not rash to answer; asks what is relevant and answers to the point; speaks of the first matter first and the last matter last; and concerning what he has not heard, he says "I have not heard [this]"; and he acknowledges the truth — and the reverse of these characterize a clod. And the sage said: whoever speaks with wisdom and sense is like salt in a dish, and there is grace in his fitting words, like settings of gold. "The wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heard" (Ecclesiastes 9:16) — let him go to a person whose words are heard and put his words in that person's mouth so they may be heard, but he himself should remain silent.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:67: The general principle of the matter: just as a person makes a door for his entrance, and it has a time to close and a time to open, so he should close the door of his mouth with the two doors of the lips and teeth. Be very careful about opening your mouth, and guard your tongue as you would guard silver, gold, and pearls within your room and within your chests; make a lock upon your lock — this is what you should do for your mouth.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:68: See how the early ones were careful about idle talk, praising themselves for never having spoken idle words all their lives. In this matter there is a great remedy for praying with intention, since most of the loss of intention in prayer comes from idle words fixed in one's heart. Also, silence is a great fence for the fear of Heaven, for it is impossible to have a heart that fears Heaven while multiplying words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:69: And with this, this chapter is concluded:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:1: Having discussed, in the preceding chapter, the greatness of silence, we now wish, in this chapter, to explain the matter of the four classes who do not receive the presence of the Shechinah, all of which depend on speech, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Sotah (42a): Rav Chisda said, and some say Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba: four classes do not receive the presence of the Shechinah — the class of mockers, the class of flatterers, the class of liars, and the class of tellers of evil speech — as it is written, "for You are not a God who desires wickedness, evil shall not sojourn with You" (Psalms 5:5). And the Zohar does not speak of these four classes together.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:2: It appears, in a general way, that these blemish the four letters of Adonai, and therefore they do not see the presence of the Shechinah. And when any of these classes causes a blemish, he blemishes the entire Name, for the four letters are all one Name; and when the Shechinah is blemished, the mystery of YHVH likewise withdraws from the Shechinah, and it follows that he cuts off the unification, and therefore does not see the presence of the Shechinah. The mystery of "the presence of the Shechinah" we shall further explain below.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:3: When you examine carefully, you will find that each class blemishes one letter: the class of mockers [blemishes] the letter Aleph and the letter Yod, and so on — thereby causing evil to himself and his soul, bringing sufferings upon himself, because the supernal flow is diminished from its source; and so, from the great heights he falls to the lowest depths, into Gehinnom; and likewise his sustenance is diminished, for from there sustenance flows — "You open Your hand" (Psalms 145:16) — [an allusion to] "Yodcha" (Tikkunei Zohar 7b) — that is, the drawing forth of His hand. The class of flatterers [corresponds to] Heh, because their essence is that they speak one thing with their mouth and another in their heart, and thus the blemish is in both together. The class of liars [corresponds to] Vav, for the letter Vav is the letter of truth, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi 241b) regarding "and you shall give me a true sign" (Joshua 2:12). The class of tellers of evil speech [corresponds to] the final Heh, and the passages we shall write below prove this — this being "this shall be the law of the leper" (Leviticus 14:2), and so on — and this hint suffices for the intelligent reader.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:4: I have heard from the name of the Kabbalists that corresponding to these four classes are four impure animals: the hyrax, the hare, the camel, and the pig. And corresponding to these there are four kelipot above, to bring up the sinner's deed and punish him in Gehinnom. Further, I have heard that whoever sinned and was of these four aforementioned classes is destined to be reincarnated into these four impure animals, each into the animal alluded to and appropriate to him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:5: Regarding the punishment of the mocker, Rabbi Elazar said (Avodah Zarah 18b): whoever mocks, sufferings come upon him, as it is said, "and now, do not mock, lest your bonds be made strong, for a decree of destruction have I heard" (Isaiah 28:22). Rabbah said to the Rabbis: please, I beg of you, do not mock, so that sufferings not come upon you. Rav Katina said, whoever mocks, his sustenance is diminished, as it is said, "He has stretched forth His hand with mockers" (Hosea 7:5). And Rav Katina said, whoever mocks falls into Gehinnom, as it is said, "the proud and haughty man, mocker (letz) is his name..." (Proverbs 21:24), and "wrath" (evrah) refers to none other than Gehinnom, as it is said, "a day of wrath..." (Zephaniah 1:15). Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai said, whoever mocks brings about destruction for the world, as it is said, "and now, do not mock, lest your bonds be made strong, for a decree of destruction have I heard." Rabbi Elazar said, mockery is harsh, for it begins with sufferings and ends in destruction — so far his words. This makes clear how much evil it causes to himself, his soul, and the whole world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:6: Rabbeinu Yonah, of blessed memory, wrote in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 3, item 174) five divisions regarding the class of mockers, in these words: mockery is harsh — for Jehu was not punished until he mocked, even though there was no wrongful intent in his heart, as it is said, "and Jehu gathered all the people and said to them, Ahab served Baal a little..." (II Kings 10:18). Mockery is harsh — for the verse specified expelling none of the transgressors except the mocker, as it is said, "cast out the mocker, and contention shall go out" (Proverbs 22:10). Mockery is harsh — for the punishment did not hasten to come upon the generation of the flood until they mocked Noah, as it is said, "he who is at ease has contempt for misfortune" (Job 12:5), and so on — Noah was before them like a torch [warning of disaster], and they despised his words and mocked him. Mockery is harsh — for the punishment did not hasten to come upon Sodom until they mocked Lot, as it is said, "and he seemed as one who mocked, in the eyes of his sons-in-law" (Genesis 19:14); they said to him, "Fool! There is revelry with drums and flutes in the city, and you say it is being overturned!" Mockery is harsh — for because of it forty-two men of Israel were killed, as it is said, "and young children came out of the city and mocked him, saying to him, Go up, baldhead..." (II Kings 2:23), and it is written, "and he turned behind him and saw them and cursed them in the name of the Lord." Sanballat and Tobiah were punished only for mocking Israel during the building of the Temple, as it is said, "and Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite heard it, and they mocked us" (Nehemiah 2:19). And whoever mocks has no remedy for his wound, as it is said, "and they mocked the messengers of God... until the wrath of the Lord arose" (II Chronicles 36:16). And even in the lightest of light matters, a person is not permitted to mock, as it is said, "He has stretched forth His hand with mockers" (Hosea 7:5).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:7: We learn in the Midrash Mishlei, on the verse (Proverbs 9:12), "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; but if you mock, you alone shall bear it": a parable of two people, one poor and one rich; the poor man would say to the rich man, "What benefit do I have from you? Whatever you acquired, you acquired for yourself." So the Holy One, blessed be He, says to the wise man: even though you acquired wisdom for yourself, you acquired it for yourself — therefore it says, "If you are wise..." Rabbi Elazar says, if you are wise in Torah, it is as though you gladden the Holy One, blessed be He, who gave it to you — this is [the meaning of] "you are wise for yourself," that is, for the One who gave you wisdom. "But if you mock, you alone shall bear it" — and not others.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:8: Further, they said, of blessed memory (Megillah 25b): all mockery is forbidden except mockery of idolatry — from where do we learn this? From Elijah, peace be upon him, as it is said, "and it came to pass at noon, that Elijah mocked them..." (I Kings 18:27). He said to them: does the Baal that you worship converse (siach lo)? Perhaps he created all the trees, as it is said, "and every plant (siach) of the field" (Genesis 2:5). Does he set boundaries (sig lo)? Perhaps he established all boundaries, as it is said, "you shall not remove your neighbor's boundary (tasig)" (Deuteronomy 19:14). Does he have a way (derech lo)? Perhaps he split the sea for you and made a way in it, as it is said, "who makes a way in the sea" (Isaiah 43:16). "Perhaps he is asleep and will wake" — or perhaps he revived your dead for you and awakens them from their sleep to the life of the World to Come? All these deeds are only the deeds of the Holy One, blessed be He; it is fitting for Him to be served and worshiped, blessed be His Name forever and ever — so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:9: Regarding the essence of mockery, there are several aspects. One of them is one who establishes himself in the corners of houses for idle talk and vain words — this is called a "mocker," for they said in chapter 3 of Avot (2): two who sit together with no words of Torah between them, this is a session of mockers, and so on — and it says "sit," even if they are not engaged in mocking talk, since there are no words of Torah between them, it is called a session of mockers; all the more so one who engages in idle talk, since he could occupy himself with Torah at that time and does not, is called a mocker.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:10: The pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, wrote regarding the reason for this, in these words: and the reason is that the punishment for its neglect corresponds to the greatness of its reward, as it is said, "and in the session of mockers he does not sit" (Psalms 1:1), and they say that the proof is from the end of the verse (Psalms 1:2), "but his desire is in the Torah of the Lord" — as though it said, because his desire is in the Torah of the Lord, he does not sit in the session of mockers, which has no Torah of the Lord in it. To me, this is a complete proof from the verse he mentioned — is there greater mockery than one to whom it is said, "a hundred gold coins per hour, and all that you count is yours," and he mocks the gold coins and disparages them? So too one who is idle from words of Torah, after knowing this great reward, is nothing but a true mocker. And so the sage said (Avot 6:2), "woe to the creatures for the disgrace of Torah" — thus he called one idle from words of Torah a disgracer — and this is exactly the point here. And when the prophet Isaiah condemned the people of his generation who were idle from Torah, he called them "men of mockery," as it is said, "hear the word of the Lord, you men of mockery" (Isaiah 28:14) — and this is a true indication of all these matters — so far his words. There is support for this in tractate Sanhedrin (99a), where they say regarding "for he has despised the word of the Lord": Rabbi Nechemiah says, whoever is able to occupy himself with Torah and does not, and so on.
